2026 SEMA Show • Toyota Brings Fresh Adventure-Ready Concepts at the 2026 SEMA Show Under the Woodland Banner
Stock Chevy Corvette E-Ray Walks Into a Speed Shop, Drives Away With 850 HP, and a Supercharger
26 photos
Photo: YouTube/Late Model Racecraft
The Corvette E-Ray was Chevrolet’s first attempt at making America’s Sportscar accustomed to the dawning era of electrical upgrades. As a result, the fabled mid-engined C8 received an e-motor for the front axle, adding 160 extra hp to the V8’s output. One thing led to another, and now the ZR1X is killing hypercars like there’s a bounty of their heads. In the meantime, one E-Ray owner has decided natural aspirations are not high enough for his expectations, and put a blower on his car.
When automotive engineers first pitched hybrid powertrains to the public, the concept was romanticized as the ultimate mechanical lovechild of the internal-combustion and electric worlds, destined to inherit the finest genes from both parents.
As it turned out, the frugal Toyota Prius was never going to be every enthusiast's cup of tea, so the technology soon adopted a fiercely aggressive persona that prioritized blistering velocity over miserly fuel economy calculations.
That philosophical transformation ignited in 2013 through three European hypercars that reshaped performance engineering forever. Ferrari built 499 Coupes of the LaFerrari, pairing a 6.3-liter V12 with electric assist for 950 horsepower (963 PS).
Simultaneously, McLaren assembled 375 examples of its 3.8-liter V8 twin-turbocharged P1 delivering 903 horsepower (916 PS), including 177 from an e-motor, while Porsche crafted 918 all-wheel-drive units of the 887-horsepower (899-PS) 918 Spyder (4.6-liter aspirated V8 plus 179 electric hp).
Photo: YouTube/Late Model Racecraft Those pioneers spawned an entire dynasty of electrified exotics across the decade. Ferrari unleashed the 986-horsepower (1,000-PS) 4.0-liter SF90 Stradale, the 819-horsepower (830-PS) 3.0-liter 296 GTB, and the 1,184-horsepower (1,200-PS) F80, while McLaren introduced the 690-horsepower (700-PS) 3.0-liter Artura and 1,258-horsepower (1,275-PS) W1.
Lamborghini answered with the 808-horsepower (819-PS) Sián, the 1,001-horsepower (1,015-PS) 6.5-liter V12 Revuelto, and the 907-horsepower (920-PS) Temerario, whereas Porsche launched its 532-horsepower (541-PS) 3.6-liter 911 GTS.
Naturally, America refused to watch this high-voltage revolution from the sidelines, and the eighth-generation Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray was born as the first electrified, all-wheel-drive model in Corvette history. Behind the cabin sits GM's naturally aspirated 6.2-liter LT2 pushrod V8, which independently generates 495 horsepower (502 PS) at 6,450 rpm and 470 lb-ft (637 Nm) of torque at 5,150 rpm while driving the rear axle via an 8-speed dual-clutch gearbox.
Photo: YouTube/Late Model Racecraft Up front, a permanent-magnet electric motor draws energy from a self-charging 1.9-kWh lithium-ion battery pack in the center tunnel for 160 horsepower (162 PS) and 125 lb-ft (169 Nm) of torque. Combined, the factory E-Ray produces 655 horsepower (664 PS) and 595 lb-ft (807 Nm) of torque, sprinting from 0 to 60 mph (97 kph) in 2.5 seconds and covering the quarter-mile in 10.5 seconds at 130 mph (209 kph).
Even with those blistering showroom credentials, a dedicated segment of the gearhead population firmly believes that factory output figures are merely a conservative baseline and that there is always room for improvement. Enter Steven Fereday and his crew at Texas tuning powerhouse Late Model Racecraft, where turning stock Corvettes into supercar-slaying monsters is a daily craft demonstrated at their proving grounds.
The subject of their latest showcase is a pristine 2025 Corvette E-Ray Coupe owned by a returning Texas customer, Greg Manning. A while back, the shop built his seventh-generation Corvette Z06 with an 800-horsepower (811-PS) package before upgrading it with a Magnuson supercharger that pulled relentlessly across the tachometer. Hooked on forced induction, Mr. Manning purchased this low-mileage 2025 E-Ray and stored it until the speed shop could work its magic.
Photo: YouTube/Late Model Racecraft Once completed with Late Model Racecraft's signature supercharger package, Mr. Manning's hybrid coupe delivers a combined 850 horsepower (862 PS) at the flywheel and around 583 rear-wheel horsepower (608 PS). That represents a reliable 150-rear-wheel-horsepower (152-PS) gain on 91-octane or 93-octane pump fuel. Anchoring the build is a Magnuson 2650 supercharger featuring a taller lid that flows enough air for 10 to 15 extra horsepower.
Fitting a roots-style blower into a tight mid-engine bay requires intricate engineering: watch Zach, the shop technician, demonstrate this before installation. The Magnuson 2650 system relies on an auxiliary jackshaft assembly that bolts onto the cylinder head over alignment pins, linking the factory serpentine belt system on one side to a dedicated blower drive pulley and idlers. Two internal intercooler bricks, an expansion tank, and an upgraded heat exchanger prevent heat soak.
Before reaching the Texas facility, Mr. Manning's coupe had already received a bespoke rear fascia conversion that reshaped the lower valance to accommodate a center-exit stainless-steel cat-back exhaust system modeled after the eighth-generation Corvette Z06. This setup allows the 6.2-liter pushrod V8 roar to harmonize with the supercharger whine. Aftermarket lowering springs drop the metallic maroon body and tan cabin over custom wheels.
Photo: YouTube/Late Model Racecraft Mechanical hardware only tells half the story, as Late Model Racecraft's proprietary calibration of the Engine Control Module and Transmission Control Module unlocks the platform's true capability. According to Steven Fereday, cracking the 8-speed dual-clutch transmission software eliminated the clutch slip that previously limited modified mid-engine Corvettes.
Furthermore, their calibration enables automatic upshifts at peak engine speed even in Manual Mode, freeing drivers from watching the tachometer during full-throttle sprints.
Out on the pavement, Track Mode on, and disabled traction control, the force-fed electro-ICE ‘Vette executes violent second-gear roll pulls from 30 mph (48 kph) at 4,000 rpm. With the front electric motor pulling alongside 600 rear-wheel horsepower (608 PS), the all-wheel-drive chassis hooks immediately in a perfect blend of electric motor hum, blower whine, and exhaust thunder.
Photo: YouTube/Late Model Racecraft Should Mr. Manning crave more within the next 12 months, further upgrades await. By installing an upgraded fuel system with E85 flex-fuel capability, a custom camshaft, and long-tube headers, Late Model Racecraft can easily push the Magnuson-equipped 2025 E-Ray well past 1,000 horsepower (1,014 PS). That's ZR1 territory, only the force-fed V8 takes its power from the crank, not from expelled combustion gasses, like in the twin-turbo ZR1.
Before concluding the test session with a ferocious standing launch, Steven Fereday notes that this 850-horsepower (862-PS) package already delivers everything 99 percent of Corvette owners could ever want from a streetable hybrid supercar. At least, until Chevrolet decides to build a better one. In the meantime, the owner of this electro-blown E-Ray Corvette is getting ready for a half-mile test run to see what it’s made of.
